You choose the right preposition where Romanian and Italian don’t match: da (dal medico, da bambino, da tre anni, una cosa da fare), a / in (a Firenze, in Italia, a piedi, in treno), di / da (una tazza di tè / da tè) and verbs with a fixed preposition (pensare a, dipendere da, fidarsi di).
to think about / to intend to
a teacup / a cup of tea
As a child, Galileo wanted to become a doctor.
I’ve been studying Italian for three years.
I think about you, but I don’t intend to come.
Everything depends on the weather: if it’s cloudy, you can’t see anything.
To use “da” in all its meanings: where you come from, since when, at someone’s place, purpose, “as” (da bambino, da amico).
To tell “di” from “da”: una tazza di tè (full) / una tazza da tè (for tea).
To choose between “a” and “in”: a Firenze / in Italia, a piedi / in treno, al mare / in montagna.
To use verbs with a fixed preposition: pensare a / di, credere a / in, dipendere da, fidarsi di, accorgersi di, riuscire a.
To recognise calques from Romanian: “mă gândesc la tine” = penso a te, not “penso di te”.
To use expressions with prepositions: su per giù, in tempo / a tempo, di sera / la sera, fra poco.
Florence, October. At a weekend science school at the Arcetri Observatory, Pietro meets Andrei, a boy from Sibiu who taught himself Italian. Andrei speaks well, but gets his prepositions wrong.
Hi! I’m from Sibiu, I’ve been in Italy since Monday. I came by train.
Welcome! Just two things: you say “in Italia”, not “a Italia”. And usually “in treno”.
In Italia, in treno. But “a Firenze”?
Yes: cities with “a”, countries with “in”. A Firenze, in Italia. A Sibiu, in Romania.
How hard. Tonight, when we look at Jupiter, I’ll think about my grandmother. She loves the stars.
You’ll think about your grandmother. “Pensare a” someone. “Pensare di” means to intend: penso di partire.
So: I think about my grandmother, and I intend to write to her. Right?
Perfect. In Romanian it’s all “la”, isn’t it? Mă gândesc la… Matei explained it to me.
You know Romanian? Then you know why I make mistakes. It depends on my language.
Dipende dalla tua lingua. “Dipendere da”. But don’t worry: prepositions are the hardest stars to see.
NN and CCH, stress on “CHIA”: can-noc-CHIA-le.
I’ve been studying for three years.
I’m going to the doctor’s / to Bianca’s.
una tazza da tè, una cosa da fare
as a child, as a friend
“Da” + time with the present: Studio l’italiano da tre anni = I’ve been studying for three years (and still am). Romanian also uses the present; English doesn’t (I have been studying).
“di” = what it contains / what it’s made of
una tazza di tè (full of tea)

“Di” also shows the author, origin or material: un quadro di Lippi, sono di Firenze (= I’m Florentine), un tavolo di legno. “Sono di Sibiu” = I’m from Sibiu (by birth); “vengo da Sibiu” = I’m (now) coming from Sibiu.
countries, regions: in Italia, in Toscana
in treno, in macchina, in bici
al mare, al cinema, a scuola
in montagna, in biblioteca, in cucina
a casa, a letto, a teatro
in ufficio, in giardino, in chiesa
There’s no complete rule for places: “a scuola” but “in ufficio”, “al mare” but “in montagna”. Learn them in pairs, like collocations.
Penso a te. Penso di partire.
I think about / I intend to
Ti credo. Credo in Dio. Credo ai fantasmi.
Non mi sono accorto di niente.
Riesco a vedere. Smetti di parlare.
Il lavoro consiste in tre fasi.
Romanian often uses “la” and “în” where Italian has “a”, “di” or “da”. The most frequent traps: penso a te (not “di te”), mi fido di te (not “in te”), dipende da (not “di”).
“Fra” and “tra” mean exactly the same; you choose by sound: “fra tre giorni” sounds better than “tra tre giorni”, “tra fratelli” better than “fra fratelli”.
Andrei lives in Sibiu, in Romania.
I didn’t manage to see the comet.
Che cosa si usa con le città?
A chi penserà Andrei guardando Giove?

The letter arrived at the end of September, a few days after the return from Sorrento, in an envelope with the logo of the National Institute for Astrophysics. It was the science school Pietro had dreamed of a year earlier, at the Researchers’ Night, and which he hadn’t been able to attend in the summer, because July had been the month of the Crusca, the Uffizi and his grandmother’s operation. The organisers had decided to repeat it in autumn, in a shorter form: three weekends in October, at the Arcetri Observatory, on the hill south of Florence, a few steps from the villa where Galileo had spent the last years of his life. Thirty students from all over Europe, aged fifteen to eighteen. Lessons by day, observations by night. Pietro had been accepted. And with him Bianca, who had applied at the last moment, without telling him, to surprise him. When he found out, Pietro was speechless. Bianca shrugged. “Somebody has to make sure you don’t ask the teachers too many questions,” she said.

Graziella took the news the way she took all important news: in silence, wiping her hands on her apron. Then she asked how many nights they would sleep at Arcetri, what they would eat, whether there was a kitchen, whether the teachers were serious people, and whether it was cold on the hill at night. Pietro answered that they would sleep at home, because Arcetri was an hour’s walk away, except for the last night, the one with observations in the open air. Graziella nodded gravely, like a general receiving a report. The next day, on the kitchen table, Pietro found two wool scarves, two hats, two pairs of gloves and a new thermos, still with the shop label on. When Bianca saw them she laughed and said it was October, not January. Graziella looked at her over her glasses. “Stars are watched at night,” she said. “And at night, on the hills, it’s always colder than you think. Galileo lived to be old because he wrapped up warm.” Neither of them had the courage to ask where she had read that.

On the first Saturday in October they walked up to Arcetri from via Maggio, through Porta Romana and along the road that climbs between olive trees and stone walls, the same road Galileo, old and almost blind, used to ride on his mule to visit his daughters at the convent. It took them an hour. The observatory was a cream-coloured building, with a large white dome on the roof and a garden full of cypresses, from which you could see the whole of Florence, from the Duomo to the hills of Fiesole. In the courtyard there were already about twenty young people with backpacks, speaking every language in Europe. Pietro heard German, Spanish, Polish, English with a thousand different accents. And then, suddenly, he heard a word he knew very well, even though it wasn’t Italian. A tall, thin boy with glasses and a jacket that was too big for him was talking on the phone in a corner of the courtyard, saying: “Da, mamă. Am ajuns. E foarte frumos.” He was Romanian. Pietro understood at once, because it was Matei’s language, the language in which Matei sang Viorica’s lullaby to Viola.

The boy’s name was Andrei, he was seventeen and came from Sibiu. When Pietro said to him, in his halting Romanian, “Bună ziua, și eu cunosc Sibiu”, Andrei looked at him as you look at an alien. Then he burst out laughing and shook his hand so hard it hurt. It turned out the world was small, much smaller than they thought. Andrei lived two streets away from Ion and Doina’s house, in the lower town, near the old station. His grandmother had been Doina’s colleague for thirty years at the Radu Stanca theatre, in the costume workshop: she cut the fabrics, while Doina embroidered them. And his grandfather, who had died recently, had worked on the railway with Ion, on the Copșa Mică line. Andrei had taught himself Italian, in three years, with films, songs and an app on his phone, because he dreamed of studying astrophysics in Italy. He spoke it surprisingly well, with a rich vocabulary and an almost perfect accent. But with prepositions he was a disaster.

Pietro noticed it from the first sentence. “Sono di Sibiu,” said Andrei, and that was right. “Sono a Italia da lunedì,” and that was wrong. “Sono venuto con il treno,” and that wasn’t exactly wrong, but it sounded odd. Pietro, who since Karl’s speech had become very sensitive to these things, explained gently that you said “in Italia”, because with countries you use “in”, while with cities you use “a”: a Firenze, a Sibiu, but in Italia, in Romania. And that you usually said “in treno”, like “in macchina”, “in aereo”, “in bici”, although “a piedi” and “a cavallo” took “a”. Andrei listened carefully. Then he asked why. Pietro opened his mouth to answer and realised he didn’t know. He thought of Bianca, who had once answered Karl “that’s how it’s said”. Bianca, next to him, smiled. “Welcome to the club,” she said to Andrei. “Italian prepositions can’t be explained. They can only be endured.”

The first lesson was given by the director of the observatory, Professor Elena Rinaldi, a small woman with very short grey hair and a voice that filled the room without a microphone. She didn’t talk about stars. She talked about Galileo. She told them that as a young man Galileo wanted to become a doctor, as his father wished, but that at the university of Pisa he had fallen in love with mathematics and had never again managed to stop thinking about it. She told them that in 1609 he had heard about a Dutch spyglass, an instrument that made distant things seem close, and that instead of buying one he had decided to build it himself, grinding the lenses with his own hands. She told them that on the night of the seventh of January 1610, pointing the telescope at Jupiter, he had noticed three small points of light next to the planet, and that in the following nights the points had moved, and then there were four. They were moons. Moons orbiting another planet. “At that moment,” said the professor, “the Earth stopped being the centre of the universe. And Galileo started having problems.”

Then the professor told the rest of the story, the one you study at school but which, told there, a few steps from Galileo’s villa, felt different. She told them that in 1632 Galileo had published the “Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems”, and that he had written it in Italian, not in Latin like all the scientists of his time. He did it on purpose, she said, because he wanted merchants, craftsmen, ordinary people who didn’t know Latin to read it too. That was also why the Church was so angry: a book in Latin was read by few, a book in Italian could be read by anyone. In 1633 Galileo was tried in Rome, forced to recant, and sentenced to live the rest of his life shut up in the villa at Arcetri, unable to receive visitors without permission. He stayed there nine years, until his death. “Think about it,” said the professor, looking at the thirty young people from all over Europe. “One of the most dangerous things Galileo did in his life was choosing which language to write in.” Bianca, next to Pietro, wrote the sentence in her notebook and underlined it twice.

Andrei took notes in a squared exercise book, in a mixture of Italian and Romanian that only he could read. During the break, while they drank a cup of tea in the garden, he showed Pietro a page. Next to each of the professor’s sentences he had written, in brackets, a preposition underlined twice: “innamorato DELLA matematica”, “smettere DI pensarci”, “accorto DI tre punti”, “girare INTORNO A”. “I collect them,” he said. “Like butterflies.” He explained that the problem wasn’t the prepositions themselves, but Romanian, which left its own in his head. In Romanian, he said, you fall in love “de” someone, and that was fine, because it looked like “di”. But you think “la” someone, you trust “în” someone, and everything depends “de” something. And every time he spoke Italian, those little Romanian words jumped out by themselves, like seeds from a watermelon. Bianca laughed. She said it was a beautiful image and that she would steal it for her next essay. Andrei blushed. Pietro noticed that he blushed every time Bianca spoke to him, and that she, strangely, spoke to him very often.

That afternoon they played a game Bianca invented, which they called “the preposition hunt”. It worked like this: Andrei said a sentence in Italian, and every time he got a preposition wrong Pietro raised his hand, and Andrei had to correct himself. If he managed, he won a point. If he didn’t, the point went to Pietro. At first Pietro raised his hand every other sentence. “Mi fido in te.” Hand. “Mi fido di te.” Point to Andrei. “Dipende di te.” Hand. “Dipende da te.” Point. “Domani vado a medico.” Hand. Andrei thought about it. “Vado al medico?” Pietro hesitated: you could say it, but something else was said more often. “Dal medico,” he said. “When you go to a person, you use ‘da’. Dal medico, dal parrucchiere, da Bianca, dalla nonna.” Andrei’s eyes widened. “So ‘da’ also means ‘acasă la’?” Pietro nodded. “Yes. But it also means ‘din’, ‘de la’, ‘de când’, ‘pentru’ and ‘ca’. ‘Da’ is the hardest-working preposition in Italian. It works more than Graziella.”

By the end of the afternoon the score was thirty-one to twenty-four to Andrei. Pietro protested that it wasn’t fair, because Andrei made up the sentences and could therefore choose the easy ones. Bianca, who was the referee, rejected the appeal. Then she suggested changing the rules: now Andrei would hunt Pietro’s mistakes in Romanian. Pietro accepted, confident, because since Matei had lived with them he had learned quite a few words. It was a massacre. In ten minutes Pietro made seventeen mistakes. He said “mă gândesc de tine” instead of “la tine”, “sunt la România” instead of “în România”, and at one point, trying to say he was hungry, he said something that made Andrei double up with laughter and which he refused to translate, even when Bianca begged him. In the end Pietro raised his hands. “All right,” he said. “I give up. Romanian prepositions are worse than ours.” Andrei, wiping his eyes, shook his head. “No,” he said. “They’re the same. They’re just different.”

On Sunday morning the school took them to visit the villa Il Gioiello, the house where Galileo had lived his last years, ten minutes’ walk from the observatory. It was a simple country house, with a small courtyard, a loggia and a garden full of olive trees from which you could see Florence. The guide showed them the room where Galileo, by then blind, dictated his last books to his disciples, and the window from which, before losing his sight, he watched the sky. Then he told them about his daughter, Sister Maria Celeste, who lived in a convent nearby and for years had written him beautiful letters, full of affection, advice and small news: the convent’s oranges, the nuns’ health, a remedy for the stomach. Galileo kept them all. She died young, in 1634, and he never fully recovered from the grief. Andrei listened with his hands behind his back. At the end he asked the guide what language Sister Maria Celeste wrote in. “In Italian,” the guide replied. “A simple, homely Italian. With a few mistakes.” Andrei smiled. “With prepositions too?” The guide laughed. “Especially with those.”

That evening, after dinner, they went up under the dome for the first time. It was a round, dark room that smelled of metal and oil, with an enormous telescope in the middle, as long as a car, mounted on a cast-iron pedestal. The telescope was more than a hundred years old: it had been built in 1925 and since then had watched the Florentine sky almost every clear night. It had seen a war, the flood of 1966, three generations of astronomers and thousands of students go by, and it had never complained, said the technician proudly, the way you talk about a faithful old dog. The observatory’s technician, an elderly man with a white beard whom everyone called Beppe, turned a crank, and with a noise of ancient gears the dome began to rotate slowly above their heads. Then a slit opened in the roof, and a strip of black sky appeared, full of stars. Nobody spoke. Andrei, next to Pietro, had his hands in his pockets and his head tilted back, his mouth slightly open. Pietro thought he had never seen him like that: without prepositions, without words, without any need to translate anything. The sky, he thought, is the only thing that is understood the same way in every language.

Beppe pointed the telescope at Jupiter, which that night was high in the south-eastern sky, brighter than any star. Then he invited the young people to look, one at a time. When it was Pietro’s turn, he bent over the eyepiece, closed one eye and for a moment saw nothing. Then, as he focused, the planet appeared: a pale disc, slightly flattened, with two thin dark bands crossing it like the furrows of a ploughed field. And beside it, in a row, like pearls on an invisible thread, four small points of light. Three on one side, one on the other. Galileo’s moons. Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. Pietro stayed bent over the eyepiece much longer than planned, until Bianca touched his shoulder. He straightened up with shining eyes. He thought of Galileo, who had seen them for the first time from Padua, four hundred and nineteen years earlier, with a telescope built with his own hands. He thought of Grandpa Aldo, who had never seen Jupiter, but had seen Florence under water. He thought that some things, when you look at them, change you forever.

Andrei looked last. He stayed at the eyepiece in silence for almost two minutes. Then he straightened up, took off his glasses, cleaned them on his T-shirt and put them back on, as if he wanted to be sure he hadn’t been mistaken. He said something in Romanian, quietly, that Pietro didn’t understand. Then, noticing that everyone was looking at him, he repeated it in Italian, slowly, choosing each word carefully. “I’m thinking about my grandmother,” he said. “She taught me the stars. When I was a child, in summer, we climbed the hill behind our house, above Sibiu, and she told me their names. She knew nothing about astronomy. She was a seamstress in a theatre. But she knew all the constellations, because her father, who was a shepherd in the mountains, had taught her.” He paused. Then he smiled. “Did I say it right?” he asked Pietro. “Penso ‘a’ mia nonna. Not ‘di’.” Pietro nodded. He had said it perfectly. He hadn’t got a single preposition wrong. Bianca, in the darkness of the dome, wiped her eyes with the back of her hand and pretended it was the cold.

The following week, between the first and second weekend of the school, Pietro invited Andrei to dinner at the trattoria. Andrei was sleeping in a hostel near the station and had been living on sandwiches for five days. He arrived at eight on the dot, in his oversized jacket, with a bunch of flowers bought at the Santo Spirito market, which he handed to Graziella with a bow so deep that she laughed. Then he saw Matei behind the counter, and Matei saw him, and for a moment neither of them spoke. Then they both started talking in Romanian at the same time, very loudly, interrupting each other, laughing, touching each other’s shoulders, like two old friends who hadn’t seen each other for years. In fact they had never met. But Matei knew Andrei’s grandmother: he remembered her from the theatre, when as a child he went to pick up his mother from work, a tall lady with scissors always in her pocket who gave him scraps of fabric to play with. When Andrei told him that lady was his grandmother, Matei sat down. “Signora Maria,” he said. “Scissors in her pocket. She made me puppets out of the leftovers.”

It was a very long dinner. Graziella, who had gone back to the kitchen a week earlier with Dr Neri’s permission on condition she worked no more than six hours a day, made Andrei the ribollita abbracciosa, hug included, and Andrei, who knew nothing about Viola’s word, was so surprised he knocked over his glass. Viola explained everything to him, very seriously, and taught him the word. Karl told him about his speech and about collocations. Matei video-called Doina, and Doina recognised Andrei at once, because she had seen him as a little boy at the theatre parties, and started crying, and then passed the phone to Ion, who asked him for news of every retired railwayman in Sibiu, one by one. Andrei answered Ion in Romanian, Graziella in Italian, and Viola in a language somewhere in between, which she listened to, fascinated. At one point Pietro realised that Andrei wasn’t getting his prepositions wrong any more. Not one. He pointed it out to him. Andrei thought about it. “Maybe,” he said, “when you’re at home, words find their own place.”

After dinner, Andrei took out of his backpack a small pair of binoculars, old and heavy, with a worn leather case. They had belonged to his grandfather, the railwayman. They all went up to the terrace in via della Chiesa, where the moon, almost full, had just risen above the bell tower of Santo Spirito. Andrei let Viola look first. He held the binoculars in front of her eyes, because they were too heavy for her hands, and explained where to look. Viola was silent for a moment, something very rare. Then she said the moon had holes, like cheese. Andrei explained that they were called craters, and that the first person to draw them was a gentleman who lived nearby, on that hill, four hundred years ago. Viola asked whether the gentleman was still alive. Andrei said no. Viola thought about it, then looked at the moon again and said, very seriously: “Then I’ll look at it for him.” Graziella, who had come up to the terrace with the coffee, stopped at the top of the stairs and said nothing. But Pietro saw that her eyes were shining, as when she looked at Aldo’s plant.

The second weekend at Arcetri was devoted to the Moon. Professor Rinaldi showed the young people a copy of the “Sidereus Nuncius”, the little book Galileo had published in March 1610, two months after discovering Jupiter’s moons, and which had travelled around Europe in a few weeks. Inside were his drawings of the Moon, made by hand, in watercolour, night after night: the mountains, the craters, the shadows lengthening at lunar sunset. They were the first drawings of the Moon seen close up in the history of humankind. Pietro looked at them for a long time and thought of Davide. He thought that Galileo, in the end, had done the same thing Davide did with paintings: he had taken something nobody could touch and translated it into another form, so that everyone could understand it. Galileo had translated the sky into drawings. Davide translated drawings into relief. That evening he sent Davide a message: “Galileo was a tattigrafo of the Moon.” Davide replied after two minutes, with a single word: “Lunagrafo.”

On Saturday afternoon each student had to present something about the sky of their own country. A Greek girl talked about the myths of the constellations, a Finnish boy about the northern lights, a Spanish girl about the Arab astronomers of Toledo. When his turn came, Andrei stood up with a sheet of paper in his hand and spoke, in Italian, about the names Romanian shepherds gave the stars. He told them that the Milky Way in Romanian was called “Calea Laptelui”, the road of milk, as in Italian, but that peasants also called it “Drumul Robilor”, the road of the slaves, because it was said that escaped prisoners travelled along it at night. And that the Pleiades, the little group of stars near Taurus, were called “Găinușa” in Romanian, the little hen with her chicks. Bianca’s hand shot up. She said that in Tuscany too, in the countryside, old people called the Pleiades “la Chioccetta”, the mother hen with her chicks. Her grandmother said it. Andrei and Bianca looked at each other, amazed. Two distant languages, two distant grandmothers, the same hen in the sky. Professor Rinaldi said it was the most beautiful discovery of the whole school.

That weekend Pietro noticed something else. Andrei and Bianca talked to each other more and more often, during the breaks, in the garden, under the cypresses. They talked about stars, books, university. Andrei wanted to study astrophysics in Padua, where Galileo had taught. Bianca wanted to study linguistics in Pisa, where Galileo had studied. They had discovered they shared an absurd passion for words that can’t be translated: she taught him “abbiocco”, the drowsiness after lunch, and he taught her “dor”, the Romanian longing that has no equivalent. Pietro watched them from a distance, with a strange feeling he couldn’t name. It wasn’t jealousy, or maybe a little. It was more the sense of seeing something that was about to change, like when you look at the sky before a storm. One evening, as they were walking down towards Porta Romana, Bianca asked him whether he liked Andrei. Pietro said yes, and it was true. Then she said, without looking at him: “I do too. But not in the way you think.” Pietro didn’t answer. But for the rest of the way he felt strangely light.

The last weekend of the school coincided with a special night. Astronomers had announced the passage of a small comet, visible to the naked eye for a few days before dawn, low on the eastern horizon. Professor Rinaldi decided to spend the whole night outdoors, in the observatory garden, with sleeping bags, blankets, thermoses of hot tea and two portable telescopes. Everything depended on the weather: if there were clouds, nothing would be visible. All afternoon the young people checked the forecast on their phones, every ten minutes, as if by looking at it hard enough they could change it. At six in the evening the sky was overcast. At nine it was raining. At eleven the rain stopped, but the clouds stayed. Andrei, lying on the wet grass next to Pietro, said that in Romanian there was a proverb for situations like this, but it couldn’t be translated without swearing. Bianca said there was one just like it in Italian. Graziella, who had come up to Arcetri with a basket of sandwiches and a pot of ribollita “for the hungry young astronomers”, said the clouds would clear around four. Nobody believed her.

At a quarter to four the clouds cleared. It happened suddenly, as if someone had pulled back a curtain: the wind changed, the sky opened from west to east, and in a few minutes all the stars appeared, brighter than before, washed by the rain. The young people woke up one after another, climbed out of their sleeping bags, wrapped themselves in blankets and lined up along the low wall of the garden, which faced east, towards the hills of Chianti. Graziella, sitting on a folding chair with a blanket on her knees, merely said: “I told you so.” At twenty past four, low on the horizon, above the black outline of the hills, the comet appeared. It was smaller than Pietro had imagined: a little luminous smudge, slightly blurred, with a thin, pale tail stretching upwards, like the mark of a brush on a dark canvas. But it was there. To the naked eye. Something that had been circling the Sun for thousands of years, passing close to the Earth that night, and then never again for another six thousand years.

Nobody spoke for a long time. Then Andrei said quietly that the comet would come back in six thousand years, and that none of them would be there then, nor Florence perhaps, nor Italian or Romanian. Bianca said that in that case it was better to look at it properly now. Pietro, instead, was looking at Graziella. His grandmother was sitting on the folding chair, with the blanket on her knees and her head slightly tilted, watching the comet with the same expression she had when she looked at the ribollita when it was perfect: focused, serious, almost stern. Pietro went and sat on the ground next to her. He asked her what she was thinking about. Graziella didn’t answer at once. Then she said she was thinking about Aldo. That once, in 1986, they had climbed onto the roof of the trattoria together to see Halley’s comet, and had seen nothing, because there were clouds, and Aldo had said: “Never mind. We’ll see it next time.” Next time was in 2061. “He’s gone,” said Graziella, “and I won’t be here. But you will. Remember to look at it for us too.”

Pietro did the sums in his head. In 2061 he would be forty-eight: an age that, at that moment, seemed as far away as the comet. He promised his grandmother he would look at it, that he would climb onto the roof of the trattoria, and that the sky would be clear, whatever it took. Graziella laughed softly. She said a clear sky can’t be promised, because it depends on the weather, and the weather depends on nobody. Then she took his hand and told him something else, which Pietro wrote that very morning in the black notebook, sitting on the low wall while the sky turned pink. “Stars,” said Graziella, “are like prepositions. Small, far away, and nobody looks at them. But without them you wouldn’t know where you are.” Pietro asked her where she had heard that sentence. Graziella shrugged. “I just made it up,” she said. “With all these scientists around, something rubs off.” Then she stood up, folded the blanket, and announced that the ribollita was hot and that whoever didn’t eat it straight away wouldn’t get the hug. Thirty young European astronomers lined up.

Andrei left for Sibiu the following Tuesday, by train, the same twenty-six-hour journey Ion and Doina had made many years before to come and meet Viola. Many people went with him to Santa Maria Novella station: Pietro, Bianca, Matei with Viola on his shoulders, and even Graziella, who had prepared him a bag of cantucci and a jar of ribollita for the journey. Before getting on the train, Andrei took out his squared exercise book and tore out a page. He gave it to Pietro. It was the list of all the prepositions he had collected in three weeks, like butterflies, each with the sentence in which he had got it wrong and the correct one beside it. At the bottom of the page, in capitals, he had written: “Mi sono innamorato DELL’Italia. Penso A voi. Torno DA voi presto. Dipende DA me.” Four prepositions, all correct. Pietro read it and smiled. Then, as the train pulled out, he shouted to Andrei from the platform, in Romanian, the only sentence he was sure he could say without mistakes: “Drum bun!” Have a good trip. Andrei, leaning out of the window, answered in Italian: “A presto!” And for once, neither of them got anything wrong.

Tomorrow I’m going to the doctor’s.
As a child, I lived in Sibiu.

Wrong: “Sono a Italia”. Right: “Sono in Italia”. With countries you use “in”.
Wrong: “Penso di mia nonna”. Right: “Penso a mia nonna”. “Pensare di” is for intentions.
Wrong: “Mi fido in te”. Right: “Mi fido di te”. In Romanian it’s different.
Wrong: “Vado a medico”. Right: “Vado dal medico”. You go to a person with “da”.

Write (26–28 sentences) the story of a night when you watched the sky (or of a trip to a new place). Say where you set off from, how you travelled, whose place you stayed at, what you thought about. Underline all the prepositions and check them one by one.

I used “a” and “in” correctly with cities, countries and means of transport.
I used at least five verbs with a fixed preposition (pensare a, dipendere da, fidarsi di…).
